Here are several proven measures an apartment building can take to lower its heating costs:

1. Conduct an energy audit  
   • Engage a qualified energy consultant or use your building’s EPC (energy performance certificate) to identify where heat is lost (walls, roof, windows, ventilation).  
   • Focus first on the weakest parts of the building envelope.

2. Improve insulation and airtightness  
   • Add or upgrade insulation in exterior walls, roof/attic and basement slabs.  
   • Seal gaps around windows, doors, piping penetrations and service ducts to reduce draughts.

3. Upgrade windows and doors  
   • Replace single-glazed units with high-performance double or triple glazing.  
   • Ensure frames are thermally broken and well sealed.

4. Optimize the heating system  
   • Install a high-efficiency condensing boiler or a modern heat pump (air-source or ground-source).  
   • Balance and commission radiators so heat is distributed evenly.  
   • Fit thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) in individual apartments and smart thermostats for centralized scheduling.

5. Implement heat recovery ventilation (HRV)  
   • A mechanical ventilation system with heat recovery captures heat from exhaust air and pre-heats incoming fresh air.  
   • This maintains good indoor air quality without excessive heat loss.

6. Central control and zoning  
   • Use a building management system (BMS) or district heating controls to adjust supply temperatures according to outdoor conditions.  
   • Divide the building into heating zones so you only heat occupied areas.

7. Regular maintenance  
   • Service boilers and pumps annually to ensure they operate at peak efficiency.  
   • Flush and balance heating circuits to remove sludge and air pockets.

8. Resident engagement  
   • Educate tenants on optimal thermostat settings (e.g., 20–21 °C in living areas, lower in bedrooms).  
   • Encourage simple behaviors like closing doors, using radiator reflectors and reporting drafts.

9. Explore renewable or waste-heat sources  
   • Install solar thermal panels to pre-heat domestic hot water.  
   • Investigate connecting to local district heating grids or using heat from nearby industrial processes.

By combining these measures—starting with an energy audit and focusing on the building envelope, system upgrades and user behavior—you can significantly improve your EPC energy class and achieve lasting reductions in heating costs.

An energy declaration (in Sweden known as an “energideklaration”) gives a building board a standardized, at-a-glance picture of the property’s current energy performance and highlights cost-effective ways to improve it.  In practice it will include:

• Energy performance class (A-G) – the building’s official EPC class (epc_egienergiklass)  
• Yearly energy use – delivered energy and, where available, primary energy in kWh/m²  
• Heated floor area (Atemp) and building type – size, number of above-ground floors and stairwells (epc_egenatemp, epc_egenantalplan, epc_egenantaltrapphus, epc_egenbyggnadstyp)  
• Description of energy systems – heating (district heating, oil, pellets, etc.), ventilation, cooling and hot water installations  
• Building envelope data – typical U-values for walls, roof and windows (where assessed)  
• CO₂ emissions – an estimate of the building’s climate impact  
• Recommended measures – a prioritized list of renovation or upgrade actions (e.g. insulation, window replacement, ventilation improvements), with estimated energy and cost savings  
• Validity and inspection date – when the declaration was issued and when it must be renewed  

Armed with this information, a building board can:  
– Benchmark and monitor energy consumption over time  
– Identify and budget for the most cost-effective energy upgrades  
– Demonstrate regulatory compliance  
– Reduce operating costs and the building’s environmental footprint

To achieve the greatest reduction in your building’s heating costs, you should begin by targeting the two main drivers of heat loss—your thermal envelope and your heating system—and then add controls and renewables where cost-effective.  In practice this means:

1.   Carry out or commission an energy audit/energy performance certificate (EPC) review.  The EPC will identify your current energy class (“epc_egienergiklass”) and show which elements (walls, roof, windows, ventilation) contribute most to heat loss.  
2.   Improve the building envelope first:  
     •  Loft/roof insulation – heat rises, so upgrading or topping up insulation here often gives a rapid pay-back.  
     •  External or cavity-wall insulation – reduces transmission losses through brick or blockwork.  
     •  Floor insulation – especially over unheated basements or ground floors.  
     •  Upgrade windows and doors – install energy-efficient double or triple glazing and seal air leaks around frames (draught-proofing).  
3.   Enhance ventilation efficiency:  
     •  Install a balanced mechanical ventilation system with heat recovery (MVHR).  This recovers up to 90 % of heat from outgoing stale air.  
     •  Seal uncontrolled air-infiltration points (cracks, service entries).  
4.   Modernize or optimize the heating system:  
     •  Replace old boilers with a high-efficiency condensing boiler or, better yet, an air- or ground-source heat pump.  
     •  Install thermostatic radiator valves and programmable room thermostats or a smart zoning control to deliver heat only where and when it’s needed.  
     •  Bleed radiators and carry out annual servicing to maintain efficiency.  
5.   Consider on-site renewable heat generation:  
     •  Solar thermal panels for domestic hot water can offset part of your boiler load.  
     •  Biomass boilers or heat pumps powered by renewable electricity further reduce fossil-fuel consumption.  
6.   Monitor and adjust:  
     •  Use energy-use monitoring (sub-metering or smart meters) to track consumption trends after each measure.  
     •  Fine-tune set-points and schedules to avoid overheating or unnecessary night-time operation.  

By following this staged approach—audit, envelope, ventilation, system upgrade, renewables and controls—you’ll improve your EPC energy class, cut heat losses, and drive down both your energy bills and carbon footprint.

Direct-acting electric radiators work by converting 100 % of the electricity they draw into heat at the point of use. That sounds very efficient – and it is, in terms of delivered heat versus electricity input – but when you look at the bigger picture they are generally one of the least energy-efficient ways to heat a building. Here’s why:

1. Point-of-use efficiency versus primary energy  
   • At the radiator: 100 % of the electrical energy becomes heat.  
   • Upstream losses: If electricity is generated in a fossil-fuel power plant, only around 35–45 % of the original fuel energy becomes electricity. Transmission and distribution add further losses. The “primary energy” efficiency can therefore be below 40 %.

2. Operating cost  
   • Electricity is usually more expensive per kWh of heat delivered than district heating, natural gas or heat pumps.  
   • Running direct-acting radiators continuously in a poorly insulated building can lead to very high energy bills.

3. Suitable applications  
   • Small or extremely well-insulated buildings where you may only need occasional or zonal heating.  
   • Summer cottages or holiday homes where heating runs only intermittently.  
   • Supplementary heating in rooms that seldom need a high heat load.  
   • Installations combined with on-site solar PV, where some of the electricity can be cost-free.

4. Comparison to alternatives  
   • Air- or ground-source heat pumps typically deliver 3–4 kWh of heat per kWh of electricity (COP 3–4), greatly improving primary-energy use and lowering running costs.  
   • District heating, biomass boilers or gas condensing boilers usually have better overall efficiency and lower carbon footprints (depending on fuel and local infrastructure).

Conclusion  
Direct-acting electric radiators are simple, have low upfront cost and no distribution losses, but they are rarely the most energy- or cost-efficient solution for whole-house heating. For continuously occupied or larger properties, a heat pump or district-heating connection will almost always give you lower energy bills and a better primary-energy performance.

Here are several practical measures you can take to get the most out of direct-acting electric radiators, both in terms of comfort and running cost:

1. Install programmable or smart thermostats  
   • Use built-in timers or a Wi-Fi thermostat to lower the temperature automatically at night and during hours when no one is at home.  
   • Fine-tune the schedule so you only heat rooms when you need them, avoiding wasted energy.

2. Fit thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs)  
   • TRVs let you set a target temperature for each radiator independently.  
   • You can maintain a lower (“eco”) temperature in seldom-used rooms while keeping living areas at a comfortable level.

3. Take advantage of off-peak electricity tariffs  
   • If your supplier offers lower rates at night or weekends, schedule larger heating periods (e.g. boosting temperature or pre-heating) during those times.  
   • Some smart meters will communicate with your heating system to optimize for the cheapest hours.

4. Improve the building envelope  
   • Draught­-proof windows and doors (seal gaps around frames, install weatherstrips).  
   • Add insulation in lofts, walls or floors where possible—this reduces heat loss and means your radiators don’t have to work as hard.

5. Optimize radiator placement and reflect heat  
   • Keep furniture and curtains clear of radiators to allow free air circulation.  
   • Install simple reflective panels or foil behind panel radiators to bounce heat back into the room instead of into the wall.

6. Use gradual rather than on/off heating cycles  
   • Rather than switching radiators full on/off, maintain a steady temperature using TRVs or thermostats.  
   • Continuous, moderate heat avoids the energy penalties of repeatedly bringing the room up from cold.

7. Regular maintenance and bleeding  
   • “Bleed” radiators at the start of the heating season to expel trapped air and ensure an even temperature across the panel.  
   • Dust or vacuum the fins/convectors regularly so that airflow and heat transfer remain optimal.

8. Zone control and targeted heating  
   • If your system or installation allows, split your home into heating zones (e.g. living areas, bedrooms, bathrooms).  
   • Only run radiators in occupied zones.

By combining smart controls, good insulation and regular upkeep, you’ll improve both comfort and energy efficiency when using direct-acting electric radiators.

Improving the energy efficiency of a domestic hot-water system typically involves a combination of better insulation, smarter controls, higher-efficiency heat sources and demand‐management. Here are the most effective measures:

1. Insulate storage and distribution  
   • Wrap hot-water tanks with a high-quality, low-conductivity insulation blanket (at least 75 mm thickness).  
   • Insulate all hot-water pipes (including underfloor or ceiling runs) with closed-cell foam or rubber sleeves.  
   • Minimize run-lengths by locating the cylinder as close as possible to major draw-off points (bathrooms, kitchen).  

2. Upgrade to a high-efficiency heat source  
   • Heat-pump water heaters typically deliver 2–4 kWh of hot water per kWh of electricity (COP 2–4), far outperforming electric resistance elements.  
   • Condensing gas boilers or combi-boilers with modern controls can achieve ≥ 90 % thermal efficiency when sized correctly.  
   • If feasible, add a solar-thermal pre-heater: solar collectors can contribute 30–70 % of annual hot-water demand in sunny climates, reducing fossil or grid-electricity use.  

3. Adopt demand-controlled circulation  
   • Replace continuously running recirculation pumps with on-demand or timer‐controlled pumps to eliminate unnecessary heat losses.  
   • Use thermostatic or programmable room controllers so the pump only runs when hot water is needed.  
   • Install temperature-controlled valves that stop the flow once set-point is reached.  

4. Lower set-point temperature and avoid oversizing  
   • Set the cylinder thermostat to 55–60 °C instead of 65–70 °C—this still controls bacterial growth (legionella) if heated periodically to higher temperatures, yet saves standby losses.  
   • Select a tank size that actually meets household needs; an over-large cylinder wastes energy through longer heat-up times and greater standing losses.  

5. Fit flow-restricting fixtures and point-of-use devices  
   • Low-flow showerheads and faucets reduce hot-water volume by 20–50 % without sacrificing user comfort.  
   • Aerators maintain pressure while reducing actual water—and therefore heating—requirements.  

6. Recover waste heat  
   • Install a drain‐water heat recovery unit (a stacked‐pipe exchanger) in showers to pre-heat incoming cold water using drained warm water, recapturing up to 50 % of the heat.  
   • Consider grey-water heat‐recovery showers or kitchen‐sink pre-heaters where local regulations and hygiene allow.  

7. Regular maintenance and controls fine-tuning  
   • Flush or descale the cylinder annually to maintain heat-exchanger performance.  
   • Check and adjust thermostats, mixing valves and boiler controls seasonally.  
   • Verify pump speeds and insulate any new connections or valves that may have been left exposed.  

By combining good thermal insulation, a high‐COP heat source (heat pump or condensing boiler), smart circulation controls and demand reduction (low-flow fixtures, heat recovery), you can typically reduce the primary energy needed for domestic hot water by 30–60 %.

Optimizing domestic hot-water (DHW) production in an apartment building typically requires a combination of system-level design, efficient equipment and smart controls. Below are key strategies you can consider:

1. Select the Right Heat Source  
   • Condensing boilers or high-efficiency heat pumps (air-to-water or ground-source) recover more energy from the same fuel input than standard boilers.  
   • Where available, tie into district heating with lower return temperatures to maximize condensing operation.  
   • Supplement with solar thermal collectors or photovoltaic-driven heat pumps to offset peak summer loads.

2. Centralized vs. Decentralized Production  
   • Centralized system with a well-sized buffer tank and plate-heat exchanger station per riser can reduce redundancy and simplify maintenance.  
   • Decentralized (apartment-level) instantaneous units eliminate long distribution loops and heat losses, but require individual service points.

3. Proper Storage and Buffering  
   • Use an adequately sized, well-insulated DHW storage tank to reduce on/off cycling of the heat source and avoid temperature stratification.  
   • Install stratification baffles or coil-in-coil designs to maintain layered temperatures, improving standby efficiency.

4. Minimize Distribution Losses  
   • Insulate all hot-water pipes, valves and fittings to reduce standby losses.  
   • Consider a low-temperature recirculation loop (e.g., 50–55 °C supply) with variable-speed pumps and programmable timers or occupancy sensors to limit run-times to peak demand periods.  
   • Balance flow rates in each riser or branch so that no portion of the loop sees excessive flow or standing water.

5. Smart Controls and Demand Management  
   • Integrate a building-management system (BMS) or dedicated DHW controller that:  
     – Adjusts storage and recirculation pump schedules to match occupancy patterns.  
     – Modulates heat-source output based on actual draw profiles.  
   • Use remote monitoring and data analytics to identify unusual consumption or system faults.

6. Temperature Control and Safety  
   • Produce hot water at a temperature high enough (typically 60–65 °C) to limit legionella growth, then temper down to the delivery point (e.g., 45–50 °C) via thermostatic mixing valves.  
   • Zone the system so that mixing valve settings can be fine-tuned per floor or apartment.

7. Recover Waste and Grey-Water Heat  
   • Install a grey-water heat recovery unit on showers or laundry drains to pre-heat incoming cold water by 20–30 %.  
   • Tie heat-recovery ventilators (HRVs) into the DHW loop in high-occupancy parts of the building.

8. Commissioning and Maintenance  
   • Perform a thorough system commissioning: verify flow rates, temperature set-points, pump curves and sensor calibration.  
   • Schedule regular maintenance on the heat source, heat exchangers, mixing valves and insulation integrity.

By combining high-efficiency generation (e.g. condensing boiler or heat pump), smart controls, distribution‐loss reduction and heat recovery, an apartment building’s DHW system can often achieve energy savings of 20–40 % compared with a conventional installation.

An energy declaration (in Sweden often called an “energideklaration” or EPC – Energy Performance Certificate) is a legally required report, prepared by an accredited energy expert, that provides a standardized assessment of a building’s energy performance. Its main purposes are to

• Inform property owners, buyers or tenants about the building’s current energy use and efficiency.  
• Classify the building on a simple A–G scale (the “epc_egienergiklass”) – where A represents the most energy-efficient buildings and G the least.  
• Highlight areas where energy-saving measures (insulation, ventilation upgrades, heating system improvements, etc.) would be most effective.  

Key elements typically found in an energy declaration include:  
• Total annual energy use (kWh per m² and year)  
• Energy class (epc_egienergiklass)  
• Heated floor area (epc_egenatemp)  
• Number of above-ground floors (epc_egenantalplan)  
• Building type (epc_egenbyggnadstyp)  
• Whether the building is owner-built (epc_egennybyggar)  
• A list of recommended energy efficiency measures with estimated savings  

By law, an energy declaration must be presented whenever a building is newly constructed, sold or leased. It remains valid for ten years, but if more than one declaration exists, the most recent (latest) one is considered correct.

Energy-efficiency improvement refers to any measure or upgrade that reduces the amount of energy a building, system or appliance needs to perform its intended function—while maintaining (or even improving) comfort, productivity or service levels. In a building context, “energy-efficiency improvement” typically means upgrading or optimizing components of the building envelope, technical systems and end-use equipment to lower overall energy consumption.  

Key aspects include:  
• Building envelope upgrades  
  – Improved insulation in walls, roofs and floors to reduce heat loss in winter and heat gain in summer  
  – High-performance windows and doors with better thermal glazing and air-tight seals  

• Heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) enhancements  
  – More efficient boilers, heat pumps or furnaces with higher seasonal performance factors (SPF)  
  – Optimized ventilation systems with heat-recovery units to reclaim waste heat from exhaust air  

• Lighting and controls  
  – Switching to LED or other high-efficacy light sources  
  – Installation of occupancy and daylight sensors, timers or smart controls to avoid wasted operating hours  

• Systems integration and automation  
  – Building-management systems (BMS) or home-automation platforms that adjust temperatures, lighting and shading based on occupancy or weather forecasts  
  – Zoning and demand-response strategies that focus energy use only where and when it’s needed  

• Appliance and equipment upgrades  
  – Replacing old appliances (refrigerators, washing machines, etc.) with models rated A+++ (or equivalent) on energy-label scales  
  – Selecting office equipment (computers, servers, printers) with enterprise-grade energy-saving modes  

Benefits of energy-efficiency improvements:  
• Lower energy bills—reduced fuel and electricity costs  
• Improved indoor comfort—more stable temperatures, fewer drafts and reduced noise  
• Reduced greenhouse-gas emissions—contributing to climate-change mitigation goals  
• Higher building value and better marketability—often reflected in a higher EPC (Energy Performance Certificate) class  

In summary, energy-efficiency improvement is about doing more with less energy—achieved through a combination of better insulation, smarter systems, efficient equipment and user-friendly controls—resulting in economic savings, enhanced comfort and reduced environmental impact.

In a single property you may find one or more of the following broad categories of premises. Each type comes with its own typical energy-use profile and thus affects the overall consumption of the building in different ways.

1. Residential Premises  
   – Examples: detached houses, semi-detached houses, terraced houses, apartments/condominiums  
   – Energy impacts:  
     • Space heating – the largest energy end-use in cold climates.  
     • Domestic hot water – showers, dishwashers, washing machines.  
     • Appliances and lighting – refrigerators, electronics, cooking.  
     • Ventilation losses – natural or mechanical systems.  

2. Office Premises  
   – Examples: open-plan offices, cellular offices, shared workspaces  
   – Energy impacts:  
     • HVAC (heating, ventilation, air-conditioning) – comfort cooling in summer; heating in winter.  
     • Lighting – especially in deep-plan buildings or where there is extensive use of task lighting.  
     • Plug loads – computers, servers, printers and other office equipment.  

3. Retail and Service Premises  
   – Examples: shops, supermarkets, restaurants, cafés, hairdressers  
   – Energy impacts:  
     • Refrigeration – freezers and cold-storage rooms can be major consumers.  
     • Lighting – shop windows, display lighting and extended opening hours.  
     • Ventilation and kitchen extraction – in restaurants or cafés.  

4. Industrial and Warehouse Premises  
   – Examples: manufacturing halls, workshops, storage warehouses  
   – Energy impacts:  
     • Process energy – machinery, ovens, presses, assembly lines.  
     • Space conditioning – especially in temperature-controlled warehouses.  
     • Fork-lift charging, dock-levelers, bulk lighting.  

5. Public and Institutional Premises  
   – Examples: schools, hospitals, libraries, municipal offices  
   – Energy impacts:  
     • 24/7 operations (in hospitals or emergency services) drive high HVAC loads.  
     • Specialized equipment (lab instruments, medical imaging).  
     • Higher ventilation rates for indoor-air quality.  

How premise types influence overall building energy use  
• Operating hours and occupancy density – longer hours and higher densities increase heating, cooling, ventilation and lighting needs.  
• Internal heat gains – appliances and people contribute to space heating in winter but add to cooling loads in summer.  
• Envelope performance vs. load profile – a warehouse with minimal insulation may incur large heating losses, whereas a tightly sealed office block may need significant cooling.  
• HVAC system sizing and control strategy – mixed-use buildings often require zoning and separate metering to match each use’s requirements.  

In an energy performance certificate (EPC) context you will typically see:  
– Atemp (heated floor area): summed over all premises types that are included in the certificate.  
– Number of floors and stairwells: which can influence heat distribution and ventilation losses.  
– Energy class (epc_egienergiklass): reflects the combined effect of all premises’ energy profiles, envelope quality, and installed systems.  

Understanding the mix of premises in a property and their characteristic energy demands is crucial when evaluating or improving its overall energy performance.

In multi‐unit residential or commercial buildings, electricity in common areas (corridors, lifts, lobbies, stairwells, etc.) is typically consumed for the following purposes:

1. Lighting  
   • General illumination (ceiling fixtures, wall sconces) to ensure safe passage  ͘  
   • Emergency and exit lighting (battery‐backed luminaires that remain on or automatically switch on during a power failure)  
   • Decorative or accent lighting in lobbies (e.g. wall washers, spotlights)

2. Vertical transport (lifts/elevators)  
   • Traction or hydraulic drives to raise and lower the car  
   • Control panels, call-buttons and floor indicators  
   • Lighting and ventilation within the lift cabin itself

3. Ventilation and climate control  
   • Mechanical extract or supply fans in stairwells and corridors  
   • Air-handling units or fan‐coil units in large lobbies  
   • In some installations, radiators or under-floor heating mats are electrically driven

4. Safety, communication & security systems  
   • CCTV cameras, intercoms and access‐control readers  
   • Fire‐alarm panels and smoke-extraction fans  
   • Mag-lock door releases or motorized door-openers  

5. Building services & ancillary loads  
   • Cleaning equipment charging points (vacuum cleaners, floor polishers)  
   • Service cupboards (lighting inside electrical or pump rooms)  
   • Automatic door-closing devices, signage illumination  

To minimize energy use, many modern buildings employ:  
– LED fixtures with dimming or presence detectors for corridors and staircases  
– Smart lift drives featuring energy-regenerative braking  
– Central building-management systems (BMS) that schedule lighting and ventilation according to occupancy and time of day  
– Emergency lighting with long-life LEDs and self-testing functionality  

In a typical apartment block, common‐area electricity can account for 5–15 % of the total communal energy bill, depending on building size, operating hours and efficiency measures in place.

Apartment buildings typically achieve higher energy efficiency through a combination of envelope upgrades, HVAC improvements, smart controls and—where feasible—on-site renewable generation.  Below are the most common measures:

1. Building envelope  
   • Wall, roof and floor insulation – added or upgraded to meet contemporary U-value targets  
   • High-performance windows and doors – triple- or double-glazed units with low-emissivity coatings  
   • Air-sealing and thermal-bridge remediation – sealing gaps around penetrations, balconies and junctions to reduce heat loss  

2. Ventilation and heat recovery  
   • Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) – transfers up to 90 % of outgoing heat to incoming fresh air  
   • Demand-controlled ventilation – CO₂ or humidity sensors adjust airflow to actual needs  

3. Heating system upgrades  
   • Condensing boilers – achieve efficiencies > 90 % by recovering latent heat in flue gases  
   • Heat pumps (air-to-water, ground-source) – provide heating and hot water with very low electricity use  
   • District heating connections – where available, using network heat often lowers primary energy use  

4. Hot water efficiency  
   • Solar thermal collectors – pre-heat domestic hot water  
   • Well-insulated storage tanks and low-flow fixtures – reduce distribution and standby losses  

5. Lighting and controls  
   • LED lighting throughout common areas and apartments  
   • Occupancy and daylight sensors – ensure lights are on only when needed  
   • Time clocks and programmable thermostats – optimise temperature set-backs in unoccupied periods  

6. Building automation and monitoring  
   • Smart metering for electricity, heat and water – enables tenants and managers to track consumption in real time  
   • Integrated building-management systems (BMS) – automate heating, ventilation and lighting based on occupancy and outdoor conditions  

7. On-site renewable energy (when feasible)  
   • Photovoltaic (PV) panels on roof or façades – supplement building electricity demand  
   • Small wind turbines or geothermal heat – in certain locations with appropriate planning  

8. Behavioural and operational measures  
   • Tenant engagement programmes – information campaigns and energy-saving tips  
   • Regular maintenance – keeps equipment operating at peak efficiency and extends service life  

By combining several of these measures—ideally guided by an energy audit or energy performance certificate (EPC)—apartment buildings can reduce energy use by 30–60 % (or more) and achieve a better EPC energy class.

In most Swedish residential and light‐commercial buildings, the largest shares of electricity consumption are typically found in the following areas (listed in descending order of significance):  

1. Space heating (where electric resistance heaters or electrically driven heat pumps are used)  
2. Domestic hot‐water production (electric boilers or heat‐pump water heaters)

4. Lighting (both common‐area and in-unit fixtures)  
5. Household appliances and plug loads (refrigerators/freezers, laundry machines, dishwashers, entertainment electronics, IT equipment)  
6. Cooking (electric ovens, hobs, microwaves)  

Notes:  
• If a building uses district heating for space and hot‐water heating, those uses shift off the electrical system and the relative shares of lighting, appliances and mechanical systems become larger.  
• In energy performance certificates (EPCs/energideklarationer), you will often see space heating (via heat pump electricity) as the single biggest “electric” end‐use, followed by hot‐water heating, then ventilation and pump systems.

Natural (or “passive”) ventilation relies on wind and buoyancy forces to move outdoor air through a building, rather than using powered fans and ducts.  Compared with mechanical ventilation, its main advantages are:

1. Energy and Cost Savings  
   • No electricity required for fans or air-handling units.  
   • Lower operating costs over the building’s lifetime.  
   • Reduced carbon footprint, especially in regions where grid electricity has high emissions.

2. Lower Maintenance Requirements  
   • Fewer moving parts and no complex ductwork means less routine servicing.  
   • No filters to change or fans to lubricate.  

3. Improved Thermal Comfort and Air Quality  
   • Fresh air enters more gently and often more evenly distributed.  
   • Occupants can control window openings directly, fine-tuning airflow and temperature.  
   • Reduced risk of “stale” air zones if openings are well designed.

4. Architectural and Aesthetic Flexibility  
   • Windows, vents and atria can become design features, enhancing daylighting and views.  
   • Integration with courtyards, wind towers or solar chimneys for passive cooling.

5. Resilience and Reliability  
   • Continues to operate during power outages or mechanical failures.  
   • Less dependence on mechanical systems reduces risk of complete ventilation loss.

6. Acoustic Benefits  
   • No fan noise, duct noise or vibration.  
   • Outdoor sound intrusion can be managed with appropriate opening design (e.g. trickle vents, louvres).

7. Environmental and Health Benefits  
   • Encourages a psychological and physical connection to the outdoor environment.  
   • Can reduce concentrations of indoor pollutants when designed for effective cross-ventilation.

Optimizing natural ventilation in a house involves both design considerations and operational practices. Below are key strategies you can apply:

1. Building Orientation and Layout  
  • Orient the longest façades toward prevailing breezes (in many climates this is along the cooler season wind direction).  
  • Arrange rooms so that “public” or living spaces face the main windward and leeward façades, and place corridors or service areas on the sides.  
  • Provide clear air‐flow paths through the plan—ideally a straight or gently zig-zag route from air inlet to outlet.

2. Window and Opening Design  
  • Cross‐ventilation: Install operable windows on opposite or adjacent walls. Even small windows opposite larger fixed openings can generate strong through‐flow.  
  • Stack ventilators: High‐level vents or clerestory windows in roof or upper walls let hot air escape, drawing in cooler air through lower windows.  
  • Adjustable vents: Trickle vents in window frames or wall grilles allow controlled background air supply, reducing the need to open full windows.  
  • Venetian blinds or louvered shutters: Adjustable slats let you maintain privacy and shade while still permitting air‐flow.

3. Roof and Top‐Floor Strategies  
  • Roof vents or ridge ventilators: Passive ridge systems allow warm air to exit at the highest point.  
  • Solar chimneys or thermal stacks: A dark vertical shaft facing the sun heats up and induces an upward flow, pulling cooler air into lower openings.  
  • Skylights with venting mechanisms: Can be opened manually or with thermostatic actuators to release hot air.

4. Landscaping and External Features  
  • Wind catchers or hooded intakes: Architectural elements that face prevailing winds and channel air down into living spaces.  
  • Vegetation: Deciduous trees on south façades provide shade in summer and allow sun penetration in winter; evergreen windbreaks on the upwind side can slow cold winter winds.  
  • Permeable walls or screens: Green walls or trellises partially break up strong winds and promote gentle diffusion.

5. Balancing Airtightness and Ventilation  
  • Ensure the envelope is well sealed to prevent uncontrolled infiltration (“cold drafts”)—this lets you direct airflow only through designed openings.  
  • Use air-tight, adjustable vents rather than relying on cracks and gaps for ventilation—this improves comfort and energy performance.

6. Operation and Controls  
  • Seasonally adjust venting patterns: In summer, open low windward and high leeward vents for maximum cooling; in winter, use limited trickle ventilation to maintain indoor air quality without excess heat loss.  
  • Automate vents or windows with temperature or humidity sensors so they open when indoor conditions exceed predefined setpoints.  
  • Combine natural ventilation with ceiling fans or extract fans: Gentle air movement enhances occupant comfort even when the temperature difference is small.

By integrating these design principles and control strategies, you can significantly improve a house’s natural ventilation, reduce reliance on mechanical cooling, and enhance both comfort and indoor air quality.

From an energy-perspective, the building’s overall energy class (as stated on its Energy Performance Certificate, or EPC) tells you how efficiently it uses energy for heating, cooling, ventilation and hot water. 5. Complementary measures: In lower-rated buildings, pairing efficient appliances with simple envelope upgrades (draught proofing, radiator reflectors) maximizes your overall savings.  

By choosing top-energy-rated appliances in any building, you reduce your operating costs, decrease environmental impact and—in the case of better-insulated (high-EPC) buildings—ensure that the relative share of appliance use remains minimal in your total energy footprint.

When you’re comparing refrigerators or freezers, energy efficiency isn’t just about the sticker price—it can save you hundreds of kronor a year on your electricity bill. Here are the key features to look for:

1. Energy-Efficiency Rating  
   •   Look for the highest possible EU energy class (A ++ + or better) or the corresponding rating in your market (e.g., Energy Star in the U.S.).  
   •   Pay attention to the annual energy consumption figure (kWh/year) rather than just the class label—this tells you roughly how much electricity the appliance will draw over a year.

2. Inverter-driven Compressor  
   •   A variable-speed (inverter) compressor adjusts its power to maintain temperature more precisely and uses less energy than a conventional on/off compressor.  
   •   Quieter operation and reduced temperature swings also help prolong food freshness.

3. Superior Insulation and Seals  
   •   Thick, high-performance insulation in the walls and door panels reduces heat gain from the kitchen.  
   •   Magnetic or silicone door gaskets that form an airtight seal minimize cold air leakage.

4. Frost-Free or Auto-Defrost Technology  
   •   Eliminates manual defrost cycles that allow frost buildup to insulate the evaporator coils and force the compressor to work harder.  
   •   Automatic defrost systems periodically melt away ice so the freezer stays at optimal efficiency.

5. LED Interior Lighting  
   •   Low-heat, energy-saving LEDs allow you to find items quickly with minimal light output—and minimal heat input.

6. Digital Temperature Controls and Sensors  
   •   Electronic thermostats with digital readouts and multiple temperature probes maintain a stable interior climate more accurately than electromechanical dials.  
   •   Some models include door-open alarms and vacation modes, which help you avoid wasting energy when you’re away.

7. Smart or Adaptive Defrost Cycles  
   •   Modern “smart” models monitor humidity levels or compressor run-time to trigger defrost only when needed—rather than on a fixed schedule—saving energy.

8. Efficient Airflow Management  
   •   Look for models with multi-fan systems or air baffles that circulate cold air evenly across all compartments.  
   •   Uniform cooling reduces hot spots and prevents the compressor from kicking in more frequently.

9. Right Size and Configuration  
   •   Buying a model that closely matches your household’s needs avoids wasting energy cooling unused volume.  
   •   Adjustable shelving and separate freezer drawers/zones let you organize contents to minimize how often you open large cold-air volumes.

10. Stand-by and Eco Modes  
   •   Some fridges/freezers include an “eco” or low-power mode that further reduces consumption if you rarely open the appliance or store only non-perishable items.

By combining a top energy-efficiency class, inverter technology, superior insulation, frost-free defrost, LED lighting, and smart controls, you’ll minimize electricity use—and lower both your carbon footprint and your utility bills over the appliance’s lifetime.

To estimate your home’s total power demand you need to identify every electrical load, note its power rating and estimate how, and how long, it is used. The procedure looks like this:

1. Inventory your loads  
   • List all fixed installations (electric heating, water heater, HVAC, ventilation fans)  
   • List all major appliances (oven, refrigerator, washing machine, dishwasher, tumble dryer, microwave)  
   • List lighting circuits and small appliances (TV, computer, chargers, etc.)  

2. Record or look up each item’s power rating (in watts or kilowatts)  
   • Most appliances have a label stating nominal power (W or kW)  
   • For lighting, multiply lamp wattage by number of fixtures in each circuit  

3. Determine simultaneous usage  
   • Not every device runs at full load all the time – apply a diversity or simultaneity factor  
   • For example, cooking appliances might not all run at once; HVAC runs in cycles  
   • Typical diversity factors range from 0.6 to 0.9 depending on the type of load  

4. Calculate peak demand (instantaneous power)  
   Peak Demand ≈ Sum of (Device Power × Simultaneity Factor)  
   Example: if you have  
     – Electric oven 3 kW  
     – Dishwasher 1.8 kW  
     – Lighting load 1 kW (diversity 0.7 → 0.7 kW)  
   Then Peak Demand ≈ 3 + 1.8 + 0.7 = 5.5 kW  

5. Calculate daily energy consumption (optional)  
   Energy (kWh/day) = Σ [Power (kW) × Hours of use per day]  
   This tells you how much energy you’ll actually consume  

6. Verify with measurement (recommended)  
   • Use a clamp-on ammeter or a whole-house energy monitor to measure real current draw  
   • Multiply measured current by the supply voltage (e.g. 230 V) to get real‐time power  

7. Add safety margin  
   • It’s good practice to size your service or generator 10–20 % above calculated peak demand  
   • This covers start-up surges (e.g. motors, compressors) and future additions  

By following these steps you arrive at a reliable figure for the maximum power your home will demand at peak usage—and from that you can size cables, breakers, generators or solar-battery systems appropriately.

Electricity bills are generally made up of several components—some fixed and some that vary with how much you consume. Here is how your actual usage affects what you pay:

1. Variable (Energy) Charge  
   • This is the cost per kilowatt-hour (kWh) that your supplier charges.  
   • Total = (Your kWh consumption) × (Your contract’s kWh price).  
   • If you use more electricity, this line item grows proportionally.

2. Fixed Charges  
   • A monthly “subscription” or “network fee” that does not change with usage.  
   • Covers metering, billing administration and a portion of the grid-operator’s costs.  
   • Unaffected by whether you use 100 kWh or 1 000 kWh.

3. Tiered or Block-Rate Tariffs (if applicable)  
   • Some suppliers introduce stepped pricing. For example:  
     – First 500 kWh at 1.20 SEK/kWh  
     – Next 500 kWh at 1.50 SEK/kWh  
     – Above 1 000 kWh at 1.80 SEK/kWh  
   • Once you pass a threshold, additional consumption is billed at a higher rate.

4. Time-of-Use (ToU) or Spot Market Tariffs  
   • With ToU contracts, prices vary by hour or season: e.g., “peak” vs. “off-peak.”  
   • If you consume more during expensive peak hours, your average price per kWh will rise.  
   • Some contracts track Nord Pool spot prices on an hourly basis, so higher overall consumption—especially at peak times—translates directly into higher costs.

5. Demand or Capacity Charges (mainly for larger customers)  
   • Charged on your highest instantaneous power draw (kW) during a billing period.  
   • If you switch on many heavy appliances at once, you can push up both your demand fee and your total energy charge.

6. Taxes and Fees  
   • Energy tax (energiskatt), VAT and sometimes a green certificate fee are calculated as a proportion of your energy and fixed charges.  
   • The more you consume, the larger the base for these percentage-based fees.

Key Takeaways  
– Reducing total kWh lowers your variable-cost linearly.  
– Avoiding high-use periods (or shifting load to off-peak times) can cut your average price if you’re on a time-of-use or spot-price contract.  
– Staying within lower tariff blocks (where offered) keeps your unit price down.  
– Lowering your peak power draw can reduce demand charges if they apply to you.

By understanding your specific contract model (fixed vs. variable rate, time-of-use, tiered pricing) and tracking both total consumption and peak use, you can better manage—and potentially reduce—your electricity costs.

A household or business in Sweden needs two separate agreements to get “power from the wall” to usable electricity on your premises:

1. Grid Contract (nätavtal)  
   • Who you sign with: The local grid- or distribution network operator (the company that owns and maintains the poles, wires and transformers in your area).  
   • What it covers:  
     – Right to connect to and draw electricity from the national or regional grid.  
     – Fees for capacity (the maximum power you can draw), energy losses in the grid, meter reading and network maintenance.  
     – Emergency response, fault management and power-quality guarantees.  
   • Pricing structure: Generally a fixed monthly fee plus a volumetric fee (öre/kWh) for grid losses and meter services. You pay this regardless of your electricity supplier.

2. Electricity Supply Contract (elhandelsavtal)  
   • Who you sign with: An electricity retailer or trader (an energy company that buys power on the wholesale market and sells it to end-users).  
   • What it covers:  
     – Purchase of the electricity commodity itself.  
     – Choice of product: fixed-price, variable (spot-price) or green-certificate-backed contracts.  
     – Retailer services such as billing, customer support and sustainability certification.  
   • Pricing structure: Depends on your chosen product – it may be a fixed tariff per kWh, a time-of-use rate tied to Nord Pool spot prices, or a premium for guaranteed renewable energy.  

Why you need both  
– Without a grid contract you have no physical connection or legal right to draw power from the network.  
– Without an electricity supply contract you cannot legally purchase or consume the energy; the grid operator merely delivers whatever flows on the grid to your meter.  

In practice you typically set up your grid contract first (with your local network company) and then choose an electricity supplier whose product and pricing suit your consumption profile and sustainability goals.

Control and regulation technology (sometimes called building automation or process control) is the collection of methods, devices and systems used to monitor, manage and optimise technical installations in a building or industrial process. Its main purpose is to ensure that environmental and operational parameters (temperature, humidity, air-flow, lighting, pressure, etc.) remain within desired limits for comfort, energy efficiency, safety and reliability.  

Key aspects include:  
• Sensors and measurement  
  – Devices that continuously record physical variables (e.g. temperature sensors, humidity probes, CO₂ sensors, pressure transducers).  
• Controllers and control logic  
  – Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), building management system (BMS) servers or dedicated control units that compare actual measurements against set-points and calculate corrective actions.  
  – Control algorithms may range from simple on/off or proportional–integral–derivative (PID) loops to advanced model-based or adaptive controls.  
• Actuators and final control elements  
  – Components such as control valves, dampers, variable-speed drives for fans and pumps, or dimmers for lighting that physically adjust the installation in response to controller commands.  
• Communication and integration  
  – Field and network protocols (BACnet, Modbus, KNX, LonWorks, etc.) that carry data between sensors, controllers, actuators and supervisory systems.  
  – Integration with energy-management platforms, fire- and security systems or remote monitoring services.  
• User interfaces and supervision  
  – Operator panels, touchscreens or web-based dashboards that allow facility managers to visualise system performance, modify set-points, schedule operations and receive alarms.  

Typical applications in a building include:  
  • Climate control (HVAC): automated regulation of heating, cooling and ventilation to maintain comfort while minimising energy use.  
  • Lighting control: daylight-responsive dimming, occupancy detection and scheduling to reduce power consumption.  
  • Water and energy metering: tracking consumption and triggering corrective actions if thresholds are exceeded.  
  • Fire and safety systems: ensuring doors, fans or dampers react automatically in an emergency.  

By applying control and regulation technology, buildings can achieve better indoor comfort, lower energy bills, reduced environmental impact and improved operational reliability.

Expanding a building-automation or process-control system typically involves one or more of the following steps:

1. Assess Requirements  
   • Identify exactly what new functions you need (e.g. additional zones of HVAC control, lighting, access automation, monitoring of new plant equipment, etc.).  
   • Determine performance requirements (response time, data-logging granularity, alarm handling, redundancy).

2. Choose a Modular Architecture  
   • Many modern control platforms (PLC/RTU/BMS) are designed to grow by “daisy-chaining” or plugging in extra I/O modules.  
   • Select controllers with spare capacity or with available expansion slots.  

3. Add I/O and Field Devices  
   • Install additional digital or analog input/output modules to handle new sensors (temperature, pressure, humidity, flow) and actuators (valves, dampers, motors).  
   • If the system is distributed, deploy remote I/O stations closer to field devices to reduce wiring costs.

4. Extend the Communication Network  
   • Use an open or standardized fieldbus or backbone (BACnet/IP, Modbus TCP, KNX, LonWorks or OPC UA) so that new controllers and devices can be integrated seamlessly.  
   • Ensure you have sufficient bandwidth and address space on your network segments; install network switches or routers if needed.

5. Update the Control Software  
   • Modify or expand your control logic (ladder diagrams, function blocks or scripts) to incorporate the new I/O points and define new interlocks, sequences or set-points.  
   • Verify that alarms and trends are configured for the newly added data.

6. Integrate with Higher-Level Systems  
   • If you have a SCADA or BMS supervising multiple subsystems, register the new controllers so they appear in the central operator displays.  
   • Update reporting, scheduling and energy-management routines to make use of the additional data.

7. Commission and Test  
   • Perform point-to-point checks on every new sensor and actuator.  
   • Carry out functional tests of all new control sequences, including safety and alarm scenarios.  
   • Tune PID loops or other control parameters as required.

8. Documentation and Training  
   • Update wiring diagrams, I/O lists and control-logic documentation to reflect the expansion.  
   • Train operations and maintenance staff on any new hardware, software tools or procedures.

By following a structured approach—defining requirements, using a modular hardware architecture, extending your network with open protocols, updating your control logic and thoroughly testing—you can scale your control system in a reliable, future-proof way.

Load balancing for EV (electric vehicle) charging refers to the methods and systems used to distribute available electrical power among one or more charging points so that:

• You never exceed the maximum capacity of your electrical supply (for example, the building’s main fuse, transformer or local grid connection)  
• Each connected vehicle receives the optimal charging current possible at any given time  
• You avoid costly grid-peak charges or penalties imposed by your utility

Key aspects of EV‐charging load balancing:

1. Static vs. Dynamic Load Balancing  
   – Static Load Balancing allocates fixed shares of the available power to each charger. For example, if you have a 40 kW main supply and four sockets, you might assign each socket 10 kW by default.  
   – Dynamic (or real‐time) Load Balancing continually measures total power draw and redistributes current among the chargers. If one car is unplugged or fully charged, the freed‐up capacity is automatically reallocated to the remaining vehicles.

2. Centralized vs. Decentralized Control  
   – Centralized systems use a master controller (often integrated with a building energy management system) to monitor and adjust all chargers. This offers the highest level of coordination and is common in larger installations such as apartment complexes, workplaces or fleet depots.  
   – Decentralized systems rely on intelligence built into each charging station; stations communicate peer‐to‐peer to negotiate their share of power. Decentralized solutions can be easier to install in smaller sites, but may offer less granular control.

3. Integration with Building Energy Management  
   – Load balancing can be linked to other building loads (HVAC, lighting, lifts) to optimize overall energy use and avoid simultaneous peaks.  
   – When onsite renewables (solar PV, wind turbines) or battery storage are available, the system can preferentially route green energy to the chargers and reduce grid imports.

4. Metrics and Communication  
   – Key parameters: total available power, maximum current per charger, number of active vehicles, state of charge requirements, and user priorities (e.g. urgent vs. normal charging).  
   – Communication protocols: Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP), Modbus, or proprietary APIs; ISO 15118 for smart-charging signaling between vehicle and charger.

5. Benefits  
   – Avoids costly upgrades to electrical infrastructure or higher utility tariffs tied to peak demand  
   – Minimizes risk of overloading circuits, fuses or transformers  
   – Improves user satisfaction by maximizing charging speed within safety limits  
   – Enables flexible prioritization (e.g. fleet vehicles first, emergency vehicles, or vehicles whose drivers requested a faster charge)

In practice, a load‐balancing EV charging installation will include:  
• A load‐management controller (embedded or separate)  
• Smart chargers or charging stations with metering and communication capabilities  
• Configuration of site parameters (maximum available power, charger priorities, charge schedules)  
• Optionally, integration with renewable energy systems or batteries to further optimize costs and carbon footprint.

Recommended general-lighting levels for interior stairwells are typically specified in lux (lx), measured on a horizontal plane at the walking surface. While requirements can vary slightly depending on national standards and the building’s function, the following guidelines are widely used in Europe (for example, under EN 12464-1 “Light and lighting – Lighting of work places”):

• Residential stairwells:  
  – Recommended maintained illuminance (Em): 100 lx  
  – Uniformity ratio (Em / Emin): ≥ 0.4  

• Office, public-access or commercial stairwells:  
  – Recommended maintained illuminance (Em): 150 lx  
  – Uniformity ratio (Em / Emin): ≥ 0.4  

Key points:  
  1. “Maintained illuminance” means the target lighting level after allowing for lamp depreciation and dirt accumulation.  2. A uniformity ratio of at least 0.4 (Em divided by the minimum illuminance, Emin) ensures no excessively dark spots.  3. Emergency-lighting requirements (often governed by other standards such as EN 1838 or local fire codes) typically mandate a minimum of 1 lx along the centerline of escape routes, including stairs, in the event of a mains failure.  

Always check your local building codes and fire safety regulations, since they may impose additional or different illuminance levels, especially for escape-route (emergency) lighting.

Improving lighting in basement areas typically means combining better utilization of any available natural light with a well-designed artificial lighting scheme. Here are several strategies:

1. Introduce and maximize daylight  
   • Window wells or light shafts – If the basement has small or sub-grade windows, install properly sized window wells or sunken light wells to increase the amount of diffuse daylight.  
   • Solar tubes (daylight pipes) – These highly reflective tubes capture sunlight on the roof and channel it down into the basement. They’re relatively inexpensive and don’t require large openings.  
   • Light panels or low-e glazing – Where windows exist, use high-transmittance, low-emissivity glass to let in more daylight while maintaining thermal performance.

2. Design an efficient artificial lighting system  
   • High-efficiency LEDs – Choose LED fixtures with a high luminous efficacy (100 lm/W or more) and a color rendering index (CRI) ≥ 80 so colors look natural.  
   • Layered lighting – Combine ambient (general) lighting, task lighting (over work areas or counters), and accent lighting (to highlight architectural features) for flexibility and visual comfort.  
   • Uniform distribution – Use linear fixtures or recessed troffers spaced to avoid dark corners. Aim for at least 200–300 lux of ambient light in circulation areas and 300–500 lux at work surfaces.  

3. Optimize controls and zoning  
   • Occupancy sensors or timers – Install motion-sensing controls to ensure lights only run when the space is occupied, reducing energy use.  
   • Dimming and scene controls – In multi-purpose basements, dimmers let you adjust light levels for different activities (e.g., workout, media room, laundry).  
   • Separate circuits – Divide lighting into zones (e.g., storage, recreation, utility) so you can light only the areas in use.

4. Enhance reflectance and finishes  
   • Light-colored walls and ceilings – Bright paints with a high light reflectance value (LRV ≥ 70 %) will bounce light around the room and make it feel brighter.  
   • Gloss or semi-gloss trims – Reflective trim around windows or beams further distributes both natural and artificial light.  

5. Meet safety and code requirements  
   • Emergency and exit lighting – If the basement is part of a public or multi-unit building, ensure emergency lighting and illuminated exit signs are installed per local regulations.  
   • Moisture-rated fixtures – For below-grade or potentially damp areas, use fixtures and fittings rated for damp or wet locations (e.g., IP44 or higher).  

By combining these approaches—adding as much diffuse daylight as possible, specifying efficient and well-controlled LED lighting, and using light-reflective finishes—you can transform a dim, uninviting basement into a bright, comfortable space.

   • Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) – Recover up to 90 % of heat from exhaust air while ensuring good indoor air quality.  
   • Demand-controlled ventilation – CO₂ or humidity sensors adjust airflow only when needed, saving fan energy.

   • Photovoltaic (PV) panels – Generates on-site electricity to offset grid use and may feed back to the network.  
   • Battery storage – Couples with PV to maximize self-consumption of solar energy.

   • Smart thermostats and building management systems (BMS) – Optimize heating schedules, monitor real-time consumption and detect faults early.

By systematically targeting the building envelope first, then heating/ventilation systems, followed by lighting, controls and renewables, you will achieve the most cost-effective improvements in your building’s overall energy performance.

Here are several strategies to reduce standby (idle) electricity consumption in shared or common‐use areas of a building:

1. Install Master-Off Switches or Smart Power Strips  
   • Fit power strips with a master switch or built-in load sensing. When the “master” device (e.g. a communal printer or AV receiver) powers down, the strip cuts power to all peripheral devices (chargers, speakers, lamps).  
   • Use smart strips that automatically kill phantom loads after a set idle period.

2. Use Timers and Schedules  
   • Deploy programmable timers on vending machines, water dispensers, coffee makers and other equipment that doesn’t need 24/7 availability.  
   • Integrate device schedules into the building management system (BMS) so that non-critical loads shut off outside peak or occupancy hours.

3. Apply Occupancy Sensors and Daylight Sensors  
   • Fit motion or presence detectors in lounges, corridors and meeting rooms so lighting and AV equipment only draw power when someone is present.  
   • In spaces with sufficient daylight, use photosensors to dim or switch off artificial lighting automatically.

4. Leverage Centralized Control (BMS Integration)  
   • Link all shared-area equipment (lighting, digital signage, AV systems) into your BMS or energy management platform.  
   • Define “off-hours” profiles that disable non-essential loads overnight and on weekends.

5. Adopt Energy-Efficient Equipment  
   • When purchasing new appliances (e.g. coffee machines, refrigerators, digital displays), specify models with proven low standby consumption or ENERGY STAR® certification.  
   • Look for devices with “zero-standby” or “eco-mode” settings.

6. Encourage Behavioral Change  
   • Place clear signage by shared equipment reminding users to switch off or unplug devices after use.  
   • Train staff and occupants on the impact of standby loads and simple habits—like unplugging phone/tablet chargers when not in use.

7. Conduct Regular Audits and Metering  
   • Use plug-in energy meters to identify the biggest standby culprits in lounges, kitchens and meeting rooms.  
   • Review your building’s monthly electricity data to track reductions and spot anomalies.

8. Consolidate and Virtualize Where Possible  
   • Replace multiple under-used printers or servers in a comms-room with a single, multi-function device or virtualized server that can enter low-power sleep states.  
   • Provide centralized charging stations for devices rather than letting many individual chargers remain plugged in.

By combining technology (timers, sensors, smart strips) with policy (schedules, training) and efficient equipment choices, you can typically reduce standby consumption in shared spaces by 30–50 %—lowering both your energy bills and overall environmental footprint.

Here are several strategies an apartment building can adopt to lower the energy consumption associated with producing and distributing domestic hot water (DHW). Depending on existing installations, local energy prices and incentives, and resident behavior, these measures can typically reduce DHW energy use by 10–50 %.

1. Upgrade the Heat Generation System  
  • High-efficiency heat pump water heaters – Use air-source or ground-source heat pumps designed for DHW (COPs of 3–4).  
  • Condensing water heaters or boilers – If you’re on gas or oil, replace standard units with condensing models to recover heat from flue gases.  
  • Solar thermal pre-heating – Install roof-mounted flat-plate or evacuated-tube collectors feeding into the DHW store. Solar can satisfy 30–60 % of annual DHW needs when sized and orientated properly.  
  • Hybrid systems – Combine solar thermal, heat pump and/or district heating boosters to maximize free/low-cost energy use.

2. Optimize Distribution and Storage  
  • Pipe insulation – Fit all hot water pipes, valves and manifolds with at least 25–50 mm of closed-cell insulation to cut standby losses by up to 50 %.  
  • Minimize recirculation – If you have a hot-water loop, use a timer or temperature sensor so the circulation pump only runs during peak morning/evening hours.  
  • Temperature reset controls – Adjust storage-tank setpoints in midseason or summer to the minimum acceptable temperature (e.g. 55 °C instead of 60 °C) while ensuring legionella safety.  
  • Decentralized booster terminals – In very large buildings you can install small electric or heat-pump boosters near remote endpoints to avoid running long hot-water loops.

3. Install Low-Flow and Efficient Fixtures  
  • Low-flow aerators and showerheads – Cutting flow rates from 12 L/min to 6 L/min can halve DHW usage per shower.  
  • Efficient dishwashers and laundry – Modern A+-rated machines use as little as 8–10 L per wash and heat internally to higher efficiency than a central boiler. Encourage residents to run only full loads.

4. Recover Heat and Reuse  
  • Drain-water heat recovery – Plate- or tube-type DHW heat exchangers mounted under shower drains can reclaim 50–70 % of outgoing thermal energy.  
  • Greywater systems – In larger multi-family buildings, consider closed-loop greywater recycling for pre-heating DHW.

5. Controls, Monitoring and Resident Engagement  
  • Smart metering and sub-metering – Track temperature, flow and energy use per riser or apartment to identify waste and engage residents.  
  • Timers and occupancy sensors – Switch off pump or reduce temperature during extended vacancy (night time, holiday periods).  
  • Resident education – Simple tips (shorter showers, only run full machines, close taps promptly) often yield 5–10 % savings. Provide posting in common areas or welcome packs.

6. Regular Maintenance  
  • Descale and service boilers/water heaters annually – Scale buildup in heat exchangers can reduce efficiency by 5–15 %.  
  • Leak detection and repair – Even small drips can waste hundreds of liters of hot water per year, translating to both water and energy losses.  
  • Check thermostatic mixing valves – Ensure they’re set correctly so that the supply temperature isn’t higher than necessary at the tap.

By combining several of these measures—especially system upgrades (heat‐pump or solar pre‐heat), distribution improvements (pipe insulation and smarter recirculation) and efficient end‐use fixtures—an apartment building can typically reduce its DHW-related energy use by 30 % or more, cutting both operating costs and carbon emissions.

Ventilation balancing (in Swedish, “ventilations­balansering”) is the process of adjusting and fine-tuning a building’s mechanical ventilation system so that every supply and exhaust air terminal delivers exactly the air flow for which it was designed. When properly balanced:

• Energy losses through over- or under-ventilation are minimised. You only move the amount of air you need, which reduces heating (and cooling) demand.  
• Heat-recovery devices (in a FTX-system) operate at their optimal design point, maximising the fraction of heat you reclaim from exhaust air.  
• Fan power consumption drops, since fans don’t have to work harder than necessary to overcome duct imbalances or pressure differences.  
• Indoor climate and comfort improve—airflow is uniform, draughts are reduced and humidity is better controlled.  
• Risk of moisture problems and mould growth decreases, because neither positive nor negative pressure builds up in sensitive parts of the building envelope.

Typical energy‐saving effects of good balancing are on the order of 10–30 % of the building’s ventilation heating demand. In an energy performance certificate (EPC), proper balancing will therefore show up as lower specific energy use for ventilation and better overall energy class (epc_egienergiklass).

   – Identify the single measures with the highest energy or cost savings per kronor invested.  
   – Include checks for air-leaks, insulation levels in walls/attics, window performance, ventilation efficiency and heating‐system condition.  

3. Prioritize low- or no-cost “quick wins” first  
   – Optimize control systems: lower flow temperatures, install timers and smart thermostats, balance radiators.  
   – Improve occupant behaviour: educate residents on thermostat settings, airing routines and energy-saving habits.  
   – Seal obvious air leaks around doors, windows and ducts.  

4. Move on to medium-cost envelope upgrades  
   – Add or top up insulation in lofts, façades or crawl spaces where payback is fastest.  
   – Replace or renovate the worst-performing windows/doors, starting with those facing north or high-wind façades.  

5. Tackle ventilation and heat recovery  
   – Ensure exhaust air heat recovery units (FTX) work correctly or consider installing them in common areas.  
   – Clean and adjust ductwork to minimize losses and maintain indoor-climate quality.

   – Evaluate high-efficiency boilers, district heating connections or ground/air-source heat pumps against budget and building size.  
   – Investigate solar-thermal panels for domestic hot water or photovoltaic panels for shared electricity – start small if cashflow is tight.  

7. Use a simple ranking matrix  
   For each potential measure, score:  
     • Estimated investment cost  
     • Annual energy savings (kWh)  
     • Calculated payback period  
     • Carbon-reduction potential  
     • Impact on resident comfort and maintenance

   – Check for government grants, municipal subsidies or environmental loans (LÅNE FSR, Klimatklivet etc.)  
   – Partner with energy service companies (ESCO) for performance‐based contracting if you lack upfront capital.  

9. Phase implementation and monitor results  
   – Package measures into multi-year action plans that align with the annual budget.  
   – After each phase, compare real consumption against EPC predictions and adjust the next phases accordingly.  

By following this step-by-step, data-driven prioritization—grounded in your EPC figures—you ensure the BRF invests where each krona leverages the greatest energy savings, carbon reduction and comfort improvement.
